scenes.tts: When you walk, your legs bend and straighten in turn. Who keeps the beat?
scenes.visual: A walking figure in silhouette, the knee and ankle bending and straightening in turn. Question: Who keeps the beat?
scenes.narration: When you walk, your legs bend and straighten in turn. Who keeps the beat?

scenes.tts: In the early twentieth century, a common view held that walking is a chain of reflexes, like falling dominoes.
scenes.visual: Title card: walking as a chain of reflexes? A row of dominoes labelled step, sensory signal, step, sensory signal, falling one after another.
scenes.narration: In the early twentieth century, a common view held that walking is a chain of reflexes, like falling dominoes.

scenes.tts: Graham Brown tested this in cats, in nineteen eleven.
scenes.caption: Graham Brown tested this in cats, in 1911.
scenes.narration: Graham Brown tested this in cats, in 1911.

scenes.tts: He cut the spinal cord to remove input from the brain. He also cut the dorsal roots carrying sensory signals from the hind legs.
scenes.visual: A cat spinal cord diagram: a cut line separates it from the brain, and cut marks appear on the dorsal roots from the hind limbs.
scenes.narration: He cut the spinal cord to remove input from the brain. He also cut the dorsal roots carrying sensory signals from the hind legs.

scenes.tts: If walking is a chain of reflexes, what should be left?
scenes.visual: Predict card: If walking is a reflex chain, what should remain?
scenes.narration: If walking is a chain of reflexes, what should be left?

scenes.tts: Nothing rhythmic should remain. Instead, the ankle flexors and extensors still contracted in alternation.
scenes.visual: Two traces, flexor and extensor, alternating bursts. Label: ankle flexors and extensors still alternate.
scenes.narration: Nothing rhythmic should remain. Instead, the ankle flexors and extensors still contracted in alternation.

scenes.tts: The rhythm arose within the cord. A network that can do this is called a central pattern generator.
scenes.visual: The cord glows. Label: central pattern generator, rhythmic output without patterned descending or sensory input.
scenes.narration: The rhythm arose within the cord. A network that can do this is called a central pattern generator.

scenes.tts: Modern work often uses a newborn rodent's cord in a dish.
scenes.visual: An isolated neonatal mouse spinal cord in a dish of oxygenated saline, with electrodes on two ventral roots.
scenes.narration: Modern work often uses a newborn rodent's cord in a dish.

scenes.tts: Drugs in the bath give a steady push, like holding down an accelerator. They carry no timing.
scenes.visual: Drug drops enter the bath. Label: steady drug push, no timing. A foot holding an accelerator pedal down.
scenes.narration: Drugs in the bath give a steady push, like holding down an accelerator. They carry no timing.

scenes.tts: Yet the flexor and extensor roots fire in alternating bursts. The beat comes from the cord.
scenes.visual: Two ventral-root traces, flexor-related and extensor-related, burst in alternation. Label: fictive locomotion, no movement.
scenes.narration: Yet the flexor and extensor roots fire in alternating bursts. The beat comes from the cord.

scenes.tts: Graham Brown proposed two groups of neurons, one driving flexors and one driving extensors.
scenes.visual: Two boxes labelled flexor half-centre and extensor half-centre, each wired to its motor pool.
scenes.narration: Graham Brown proposed two groups of neurons, one driving flexors and one driving extensors.

scenes.tts: Each group inhibits the other. Activity switches when the active group's inhibition fades, or the held-down group escapes.
scenes.visual: Red arrows between the boxes. One box is active and holds the other down; its inhibition fades, or the held-down box recovers and fires anyway, and activity switches across.
scenes.narration: Each group inhibits the other. Activity switches when the active group's inhibition fades, or the held-down group escapes.

scenes.tts: It is reciprocal inhibition laid out in time. Whether real rhythm comes from such a simple pair is still debated.
scenes.visual: The two pools' voltage bars go up and down in turn. Label: reciprocal inhibition laid out in time. Small tag: still debated.
scenes.narration: It is reciprocal inhibition laid out in time. Whether real rhythm comes from such a simple pair is still debated.

scenes.tts: Sensory input still matters. In newborn mouse cords, ankle nerve pulses between flexor bursts could start a flexor burst early.
scenes.visual: The alternating traces again. A pulse train is delivered to an ankle nerve between flexor bursts; the next flexor burst arrives early, shifting the cycles after it.
scenes.narration: Sensory input still matters. In newborn mouse cords, ankle nerve pulses between flexor bursts could start a flexor burst early.

scenes.tts: The cord makes the rhythm, and the senses adjust its timing.
scenes.visual: Card: the cord makes the rhythm; sensory input can reset its timing.
scenes.narration: The cord makes the rhythm, and the senses adjust its timing.

scenes.tts: Which spinal neurons make the rhythm is still open. So is how much of this holds for human walking.
scenes.visual: Two open-question cards: Which spinal neurons make the rhythm? How much holds for human walking?
scenes.narration: Which spinal neurons make the rhythm is still open. So is how much of this holds for human walking.

scenes.tts: The cord can keep the beat by itself. That beat reaches muscle as current, pushing pools up and down in turn.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: The spinal cord can make the walking rhythm. It reaches muscle as current pushing flexor and extensor pools up and down in turn. Voltage bars: flexor bars rise while extensor bars fall, then they swap.
scenes.narration: The cord can keep the beat by itself. That beat reaches muscle as current, pushing pools up and down in turn.
